note.explanation: Stability depends on where an object's centre of gravity is and how wide its base is. A low centre of gravity and a wide base make toppling less likely.
examples: A low armchair is more stable than a high chair because its centre of gravity is lower.
A bus carrying heavy loads on its floor has a lower centre of gravity than one carrying those loads on its roof.
note.checkAnswer: Lower its centre of gravity or widen its base.
note.simple: An object is harder to tip over when its weight is low down or spread over a wider base.
note.checkQuestion: How can you improve the stability of an object?
note.title: Improving stability
steps: Put heavy parts or loads as low as possible.
Make the base wider if the design allows.
If an object tilts, consider whether its weight and the ground's reaction form a turning couple that will topple it.
note.answer: Improve stability by lowering the centre of gravity or widening the base.

modelAnswer: Stability depends on the position of the centre of gravity and the base of support.
An object is more likely to topple when its centre of gravity is raised; lowering it improves stability.

A bus carrying heavy loads on its floor has a lower centre of gravity than one carrying the same loads on its top.
Widening the base also improves stability and makes the object less likely to topple.

example.question: A bus can be stable or unstable depending on how it is loaded. Explain how placing its heavy loads on the floor affects its stability.
example.answer: Heavy loads on the floor lower the bus's centre of gravity. If it is disturbed slightly, a torque brings it back to its original position, so the bus is in stable equilibrium.

explain.title: Centre of gravity affects stability
explain.body: Your textbook says: “The position of centre of gravity is very important when we are talking about stability.” A low centre of gravity makes an object more stable than a high one. This is why a low armchair is more stable than a high chair.

explain.title: Loading a bus
explain.body: When heavy loads are placed on the floor of a bus, its centre of gravity is low. If the bus is disturbed slightly, a torque brings it back to its original position, so it is in stable equilibrium. If heavy steel sheets are placed on top, the centre of gravity is raised and the bus is near unstable equilibrium; a couple can turn it over if it is slightly tilted.

explain.title: Two ways to improve stability
explain.body: Your textbook states: “We can improve the stability of a system either by lowering the centre of gravity or by widening the base.” Apply these two ideas when explaining why an object is more or less likely to topple.

explain.title: A tilted chair
explain.body: When the chair is tilted back on its legs, its weight and the ground's reaction form a clockwise couple. The textbook says this couple tends to overturn the chair backward.

mistakes: Saying that a high centre of gravity improves stability; it makes an object easier to topple.
Giving only one of the two principles when asked for both: lowering the centre of gravity and widening the base.
Saying that a bus with loads on top is more stable; the loads raise its centre of gravity.
Naming an example without explaining how the centre of gravity or base affects stability.
Confusing the tilted chair's overturning couple with a force that restores the chair upright.
